title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
Introduction
The previous three chapters dealt with social platforms: how society organises itself into a network, how those networks became digital platforms, and how to analyse them through metrics and folksonomy. This chapter opens a new block, dedicated to collaborative platforms, whose object of study is no longer the social network itself, but the group work it can support.
Before designing or evaluating any collaborative system, it is necessary to understand that collaboration is not a vague or purely intuitive phenomenon: it can be modelled, that is, described through formal theories and models that help explain why people collaborate, what collaboration requires, and where it tends to fail. This chapter presents five such models: Game Theory, Activity Theory, the 3C Collaboration Model, Tuckman’s Model, which describes the stages of a group’s development, and a collaboration ontology that integrates the previous concepts (Fuks et al. 2011; Vivacqua and Garcia 2011).
crumbs: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.1 Why Model Collaboration?
A scientific model is an abstract, logical or mathematical representation of a phenomenon, built to explain, analyse and predict that phenomenon systematically (Fuks et al. 2011). One of the best-known ways to define a model is through a mathematical formula, but models can also be graphical, diagrams or schemes, like the ones that follow. Modelling collaboration means that, instead of deciding by intuition how to support a group’s work, it becomes possible to analyse what kind of work is being done, compare different situations using the same concepts, and choose or design collaborative systems based on that analysis.
The models presented in this chapter answer different, but complementary, questions:

Game Theory explains why it is rational to collaborate, or not to collaborate, when each participant’s outcome also depends on the decisions of others.
Activity Theory explains how a human being, individually or in a group, carries out an activity mediated by tools, within a community governed by rules.
The 3C Model breaks down any collaborative work into three dimensions, communication, coordination and cooperation, which any system supporting collaboration must address.
The Collaboration Ontology integrates these concepts into a network of common terms, useful for those designing collaborative systems.

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.2 Game Theory
Game Theory studies scenarios of strategic decision-making, in which each participant’s final outcome depends not only on their own decision, but also on the decisions of the other participants. Each player chooses their strategy after assessing the opponents’ situation and anticipating the strategies they might adopt (Fuks et al. 2011). The theory originates in mathematics and economics, and its first studies date back to the 18th century, but it was mainly from the publication of The Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, by John von Neumann and Oscar Morgenstern in 1944, and the notion of equilibrium proposed by John Nash in the 1950s, that it consolidated as an autonomous field.
A central concept for classifying these scenarios is the sum of all players’ gains. In a zero-sum game, one player’s gain corresponds exactly to the others’ loss, the total sum always remains equal to zero: this is the case of a game of chess, or a hand of poker. In a non-zero-sum game, the overall outcome can vary depending on the decisions made: it is possible for all players to gain, or lose, together. As shown below, the Prisoner’s Dilemma is a classic example of a non-zero-sum game.

4.2.1 The Prisoner’s Dilemma
The best-known example of Game Theory applied to collaboration is the Prisoner’s Dilemma, formalised by mathematician Albert W. Tucker. Two suspects are arrested by the police and interrogated in separate rooms, unable to communicate with each other. There is not enough evidence to convict them of a major crime, only a minor charge, unless one of them confesses. Each is offered the same deal:

If both stay silent, each serves 6 months in prison.
If one confesses and the other stays silent, the one who confesses goes free and the one who stays silent serves 10 years.
If both confess, each serves 6 years.







Figure 4.1: The two suspects, in separate cells and unable to communicate with each other, each weigh up whether to confess or stay silent.



These four situations form the game’s payoff matrix (Figure 4.2). Analysed individually, the best strategy for either suspect is to confess: if the accomplice stays silent, confessing sets them free immediately; if the accomplice also confesses, confessing still gives a lighter sentence than staying silent alone. The paradox is that, if both reason this way, each individually rational, both confess and serve 6 years, an outcome worse for both than if they had collaborated and both stayed silent, serving only 6 months (Fuks et al. 2011).






Figure 4.2: The Prisoner’s Dilemma payoff matrix: each suspect’s outcome depends on their own decision and on their accomplice’s decision.



The Prisoner’s Dilemma shows how Game Theory supports understanding of real collaboration situations: it clarifies concepts such as self-interest, payoff matrix and non-zero-sum games. It applies to scenarios as diverse as negotiation between competing companies, management of a resource shared by several users, or the decision whether or not to contribute to a collective project.


4.2.2 Tit-for-Tat: the Evolution of Collaboration
If, in isolation, the Prisoner’s Dilemma suggests that confessing, betraying the accomplice, is always the rational strategy, the situation changes when the same game is repeated several times between the same participants. In the 1970s, political scientist Robert Axelrod organised competitions in which researchers submitted strategies for repeated versions of the Prisoner’s Dilemma, competing against each other over many rounds. The winning strategy, named tit-for-tat, was proposed by mathematician Anatol Rapoport and follows just three rules (Axelrod 1984):

Contribute first: never be the first to betray.
If you are betrayed, retaliate on the next round.
After retaliating, be willing to forgive and collaborate again.

In a repeated version of the game, collaborating stops being irrational: the expectation of meeting the same opponent again gives betrayal a future cost, the other player’s retaliation. Tit-for-tat has proven, in repeated simulations, more effective in the long run than purely selfish strategies, and is used to this day to explain how collaboration can emerge and sustain itself in a competitive scenario, without any central authority imposing cooperation (Axelrod 1984). The same logic helps explain phenomena as distinct as informal trade agreements between companies or the reciprocity observed in the behaviour of various social animals.


4.2.3 The Tragedy of the Commons
Not every collaboration-related game involves just two players. The Tragedy of the Commons, described by ecologist Garrett Hardin in 1968 (Hardin 1968), illustrates what happens when several participants share a common, limited resource.
Imagine a pasture shared by several herders, each with their own flock. For each herder, individually, adding one more sheep to their flock is always advantageous: the profit from that extra sheep is entirely their own, while the cost of wear on the pasture is shared among all the herders who use it. Since this reasoning holds for any herder, all tend to add as many animals as they can. At a certain point, however, the total number of animals exceeds the pasture’s capacity to regenerate: the grass stops growing, stops feeding any animal, and every herder loses out, including those who had been more restrained.
The Tragedy of the Commons shows that, when the gain from an individual decision is private but the cost is shared by the whole group, the sum of each participant’s rational decisions can destroy the very resource everyone depends on. For this reason, sustainable collaboration around a shared resource rarely survives on goodwill alone: it requires explicit rules, accepted by the whole group, and mechanisms that penalise those who break them, from social disapproval to formal sanctions, such as fines or exclusion from the group. It is precisely this role of rules as an element of collaboration that Activity Theory, discussed next, formalises.

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.3 Activity Theory
While Game Theory focuses on strategic decision-making, Activity Theory explains how human beings carry out activities in everyday situations, individually and in society, and is particularly useful for understanding technology-mediated collaboration (Fuks et al. 2011).
In this theory, activity is the minimal unit of meaning for understanding the actions of a subject, a person or a group, who acts upon an object, something concrete like a document, or abstract like a decision to be made, in order to achieve a goal. A central concept of the theory is that this action is never direct: it is always mediated by artefacts, physical tools, such as a computer, or cognitive ones, such as a language or a mathematical notation. The artefact acts upon the object, but also has a reverse effect on the subject itself, shaping how they think and solve problems (Fuks et al. 2011).
From a collective perspective, the subject does not act in isolation: they are embedded in a community. This collective dimension adds two new mediating elements: division of labour, which organises how the object is transformed into an outcome among the community’s various subjects, and rules, implicit or explicit norms, conventions and social relations established within the community. The complete model, adapted from Yrjö Engeström (Engeström 1987), is shown in Figure 4.3.






Figure 4.3: Activity Model: a subject acts upon an object to achieve an outcome, always mediated by artefacts; in the collective dimension, this action is also mediated by the community’s division of labour and rules.



An example applied to the classroom illustrates the model: the subject is a student or a group of students; the object is the problem or work to be done; the artefact is the computer system, the computer, or even the language used to communicate; the community is the class; the division of labour is how the group work’s tasks are split up; and the rules are, for example, the assessment criteria set by the lecturer. Introducing a new artefact, such as a collaborative platform, changes how the activity is carried out, which can create new problems but also new possibilities, and it is precisely here that the design of collaborative systems comes in.

4.3.1 Example: the Final-Year Trip
To apply the model to a concrete situation, one starts from a description and looks, in each sentence, for the element of the model it corresponds to. Consider the following situation:

The 40 final-year students of a class want to go on a final-year trip in May. Four classmates, Ana, Bruno, Carla and Duarte, form the committee that will organise the trip. The committee creates a WhatsApp group with the whole class and a shared spreadsheet to record who has already paid. The class agrees on three rules: every decision is voted on in a WhatsApp poll, the trip may not cost more than €350 per person and the fee must be paid by 15 March. The committee splits the work: Ana handles accommodation, Bruno transport, Carla payments and Duarte activities. By April, the trip is booked and paid for.

Figure 4.4 shows the model filled in with this situation. Each element is justified as follows:

Subject: the committee of four final-year students, because they are the ones who act. The class as a whole is not the subject: it only votes and pays.
Object: organising the trip, what the committee works on for months.
Outcome: the trip booked and paid for, what the object turns into at the end of the activity. The object is what is being worked on; the outcome is what is obtained.
Artefacts: the WhatsApp group, with its polls, and the shared spreadsheet. The committee does not act directly on the trip, it acts through these tools.
Community: the 40 final-year students of the class, the group the committee belongs to and works for.
Rules: decisions by vote, the €350 per person limit and the payment deadline, all agreed by the community.
Division of labour: accommodation for Ana, transport for Bruno, payments for Carla and activities for Duarte.







Figure 4.4: The Activity Model applied to organising a final-year trip: each element of the model corresponds to a concrete part of the situation.



The example also shows the reverse effect of the artefact on the subject. With WhatsApp polls, the committee stops deciding through long discussions and starts deciding by vote: the tool chosen to organise the trip changes the very way the group makes decisions.

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.4 The 3C Collaboration Model
The 3C Collaboration Model analyses any group work along three dimensions: communication, coordination and cooperation. It originates in a classification proposed by Ellis, Gibbs and Rein in 1991 for group work support systems (Ellis, Gibbs, and Rein 1991), later formalised as a model in its own right:

Communication: the exchange of messages between people, through which agreements are negotiated and commitments are made.
Coordination: the management of people, activities and resources, so that the work of several participants fits together without conflict or wasted effort.
Cooperation: joint action within the shared workspace, for the actual production of objects or information.

These three dimensions are not independent: they interrelate so that collaboration can happen (Figure 4.5). By communicating, participants make decisions that require coordination; by coordinating, they reorganise tasks that may require new communication; and effective cooperation in the shared space generates information that feeds back into both coordination and communication.






Figure 4.5: The 3C Collaboration Model: communication, coordination and cooperation interrelate so that group work can happen.



Collaboration is not the only way to organise group work. An alternative model, typical of military organisations and the classic industrial assembly line, is Command and Control (C2): a central authority decides what must be done and defines all tasks in advance, replacing distributed coordination with direct supervision, and virtually eliminating the need for communication and negotiation among those carrying out the work. For group work to be genuinely characterised as collaboration, rather than merely the coordinated execution of orders, communication, coordination and cooperation must all, in fact, take place, as represented in the 3C Model.

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.6 Collaboration Ontology
The previous models explain different aspects of collaboration, but sometimes use different terms and levels of detail. An ontology is the description of a domain, negotiated by a community, for a given purpose: it creates a common terminological base, which makes communication easier for those working in the field and allows computer systems to produce intelligible information about that domain (Vivacqua and Garcia 2011).
Building on the same model by Ellis and colleagues used in the 3C Model (Ellis, Gibbs, and Rein 1991), the collaboration ontology is organised into four parts, each with a central concept (Vivacqua and Garcia 2011): group formation, communication, coordination and cooperation.

4.6.1 Group Formation
The central element of this part is the participant. A participant takes on tasks, is part of a group and takes part in the negotiations that define shared goals; to do so, they require two essential things: trust, the willingness to depend on the other participants, accepting exposure to what they do, based on the expectation that they will keep the commitments they have made (Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman 1995; Rousseau et al. 1998), and motivation, without which one is unlikely to commit to a proposal.
Trust is distinct from beliefs, another attribute of the participant in the ontology.






Belief ≠ Trust




Belief: what the participant thinks, about the work and about their colleagues, for example, that a colleague is competent.
Trust: the willingness to depend on that colleague; it rests on the belief.
Example: believing that a colleague is competent and still not handing over part of the work to them. There is belief, but no trust.



The group, in turn, carries out an activity that generates a product, and that product is itself a kind of goal (Figure 4.7).






Figure 4.7: Ontology of group formation: the participant as the central element, with their attributes (beliefs, trust, competence, motivation) and their relationships with the group, goals and tasks.





4.6.2 Communication
The central element is the message. A sender encodes and sends a message, which follows a communication protocol shared with the receiver, and which the receiver receives and interprets; both also share a common sense that makes interpretation possible. The message also has three attributes that shape it: form (linguistic, symbolic, bodily, among others), transmission medium (from face-to-face to a computer system) and synchronism (synchronous or asynchronous). It is through the message that negotiation takes place, and it is from it that participants’ commitments result (Figure 4.8).






Figure 4.8: Ontology of communication: the message as the central element, encoded by the sender and interpreted by the receiver, shaped by form, transmission medium and synchronism.





4.6.3 Coordination
The central element is the work plan, supported by the collaborative system and established through negotiation. The work plan defines each participant’s roles and the coupling between activities, and also defines policies, deadlines and resource allocation, organising the activity into concrete tasks. Monitoring tracks deadline compliance and each task’s completion status, which in turn requires the resources needed to carry it out (Figure 4.9).






Figure 4.9: Ontology of coordination: the work plan as the central element, defining roles, policies, deadlines and tasks, and supported by monitoring of its progress.





4.6.4 Cooperation
The central element is the activity, carried out by a group with a given geographical distribution (co-located or remote) and a given degree of coupling between participants. The activity is carried out in a shared workspace, and generates a product, made up of concrete artefacts. This production breaks down into tasks, which require resources and which can be individual or shared by several participants at once (Figure 4.10).






Figure 4.10: Ontology of cooperation: the activity as the central element, carried out in a shared space and producing artefacts through tasks that require resources.





4.6.5 Ontology Summary
Figure 4.11 summarises these four parts: collaboration happens when motivated participants group around a shared goal, communicate through messages to negotiate tasks and make commitments, coordinate work through a plan that organises those tasks, and cooperate, producing artefacts in a shared space. Without any one of these four elements, collaboration is unlikely to happen (Vivacqua and Garcia 2011).






Figure 4.11: Summary of the collaboration ontology: the four blocks, group formation, communication, coordination and cooperation, and each one’s respective central concept.



A collaboration ontology is especially useful for those designing collaborative systems: it helps check that important aspects of group work, such as trust between participants or the existence of an explicit work plan, are not being overlooked in the design of a new system.

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.7 Summary
This chapter presented five models that underpin the study of collaboration:

Game Theory distinguishes zero-sum games, in which one player’s gain implies an equivalent loss for another, from non-zero-sum games, in which the overall outcome can vary; the Prisoner’s Dilemma is an example of the latter, and shows that an individually rational decision can be collectively worse than collaborating (Fuks et al. 2011)
In repeated versions of the game, the tit-for-tat strategy shows how collaboration can emerge and sustain itself without central authority (Axelrod 1984)
The Tragedy of the Commons shows that the sum of individually rational decisions can destroy a shared resource, justifying the need for rules and penalties in collaboration (Hardin 1968)
Activity Theory describes how a subject acts upon an object, always mediated by artefacts and, in the collective dimension, also by the community’s division of labour and rules (Engeström 1987)
The 3C Model breaks collaboration down into communication, coordination and cooperation, distinguishing it from the Command and Control model (Ellis, Gibbs, and Rein 1991)
Tuckman’s Model shows that a group changes over time, going through five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning; in each stage one of the 3C Model dimensions matters most (Tuckman 1965; Tuckman and Jensen 1977)
The Collaboration Ontology integrates these concepts, assigning a central element to each of the four parts: participant, message, work plan and activity (Vivacqua and Garcia 2011)

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
text:
4.8 Food for Thought
Think of a piece of group work you took part in recently: can you identify, in that work, the three Cs, communication, coordination and cooperation? Was any one of them clearly weaker than the others, and what concrete problems did that cause?
And what about tit-for-tat: can you think of a relationship, at work, in friendship or between organisations, in which collaboration is sustained precisely because the parties expect to interact again in the future? Can you also think of an example of the Tragedy of the Commons that you have observed, and what rules or penalties, formal or informal, exist, or should exist, to prevent it?

title: 4  Theories and Models of Collaboration
section: 4.5 Tuckman’s Model: How a Group Develops
text:
4.5 Tuckman’s Model: How a Group Develops
The previous models describe collaboration at a given moment, but a group is not static: it changes over time. A work group is not just a collection of individuals: its members interact and influence one another, establish social relationships and develop their own way of carrying out tasks to achieve shared goals. A group like this is not born ready. Tuckman’s Model describes the successive stages that a small, task-oriented group goes through, from its formation to its dissolution (Fuks et al. 2011).
The model was proposed by Bruce Tuckman in 1965, based on an analysis of 50 articles on small groups, and initially described four stages (Tuckman 1965). In 1977, in a review carried out with Mary Ann Jensen, a fifth stage was added: adjourning (Tuckman and Jensen 1977). Figure 4.6 shows the five stages.






Figure 4.6: Tuckman’s Model: the five stages of a small group’s development, what is defined in each, the role of leadership and the movement of the members and the 3C Model dimension that matters most in each; stages adapted from Fuks et al. (2011).




Forming: the group comes together. For an individual to become part of it, they must share its goals, tasks and way of working, identify with the others and feel part of the group. At this stage, members avoid conflict so that the group can consolidate.
Storming: with the goals defined, each member’s role must be decided. This happens through confrontation, and this is the stage with the most conflict. It ends with roles and responsibilities assigned and a leadership established.
Norming: the group defines its work process, suited to the roles assigned and to the goals. There is less conflict, because members already know each other’s abilities, and the leader plays a strong part in defining how tasks are carried out.
Performing: this is the stage of highest productivity and least conflict. Members are committed to the goals, roles and process, and the group works on its own, adjusting the process when the work requires it. The need for supervision is minimal and there is a sense of loyalty among members.
Adjourning: the group breaks up because the work process has ended, either because the task is complete or because the group gave up. What was achieved is acknowledged, the commitment to the tasks ends and the members go their separate ways.

The icons at the bottom of the figure summarise the members’ movement at each stage: they converge when forming, clash when storming, line up when norming, move forward together when performing and separate when adjourning. The role of leadership also changes across the stages: it emerges during storming, is strong during norming and intervenes less and less during performing, as the group gains autonomy.
As a group changes over time, so does the relative importance of each dimension of the 3C Model (Section 4.4), as the 3C row of Figure 4.6 shows. During forming and storming, communication matters most: members need to get to know each other, share goals and negotiate roles. During norming, coordination matters most, because the group sets its process, deadlines and distribution of tasks. During performing, cooperation matters most: joint production in the shared space, with little need for supervision. All three dimensions are present at every stage; what changes is which one demands the most attention and, with it, the tools the group needs most at each moment. This correspondence comes from combining the two models and is not part of Tuckman’s original formulation.
The final-year trip committee described in Section 4.3.1 goes through these stages. When forming, four classmates volunteer and agree on what they want to achieve. When storming, they argue over who takes each task and who coordinates. When norming, they agree on how to decide, by poll, and how to record payments. When performing, each one handles their own part without needing reminders. After the trip, the committee adjourns.

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
text:
Introduction
The previous chapter introduced, alongside the social graph, a second model for organising information in social networks: the interest graph, in which the relevant proximity is no longer between people, but between a person and the topics they interact with (Section 2.2.1). This chapter develops that idea in two complementary directions. First, it presents Social Network Analysis: its purpose, the method that turns a set of relationships between people into a sociogram, and the concrete metrics that answer questions such as “who is most influential in this network?”, “who links groups that would otherwise not communicate?” or “how cohesive is this community?”. A complete example, followed from start to finish, shows how each metric is calculated and, above all, how it is interpreted. Then, it explores the other side of the coin, the organisation of content by topic, through folksonomy, the collective classification that today structures practically every social network through hashtags.
crumbs: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
section: 3.1 Social Network Analysis: Purpose and Method
text:
3.1 Social Network Analysis: Purpose and Method
Social Network Analysis (SNA) studies the relationships between people, rather than people in isolation. Most social studies describe each individual by their own characteristics: age, education, income, opinions. Network analysis adds a further question: who each person is connected to, and what place they occupy within that set of relationships (Wasserman and Faust 1994).
This question matters because a person’s position in the network has practical consequences. Two students of the same age, on the same degree and with the same marks can have very different experiences: one knows classmates from several groups and is among the first to hear about an internship or a grant; the other only relates to a small group and rarely receives new information. None of the individual characteristics explains this difference; what explains it is the structure of relationships.
Network analysis began with Moreno’s sociograms (Moreno 1934), drawn by hand to study small groups, such as school classes. Digital platforms changed the scale: every connection, follower or message is recorded automatically, which makes it possible today to analyse networks of millions of people.

3.1.1 What it is for
The questions network analysis answers arise in very different contexts:

Education: identifying students nobody chooses to work with, understanding whether a class is fragmented into closed groups, forming more balanced work teams.
Organisations: discovering who, in practice, moves information between departments, regardless of the formal organisation chart, and what knowledge is lost if that person leaves.
Public health: predicting where a contagious disease will spread fastest and who should be vaccinated or informed first.
Digital platforms: suggesting “people you may know”, identifying influential accounts, detecting coordinated networks of fake accounts that artificially amplify a message.

In all these cases, the answer does not lie in people’s attributes, but in the way they are connected.


3.1.2 The method in five steps
A social network analysis generally follows five steps:

Define the question and the boundary of the network. Which relationship is of interest (friendship, collaboration, message exchange, co-authorship) and who belongs to the network (a class, a department, the followers of an account). The same class produces very different networks if the question is “who do you have lunch with?” or “who do you ask for help when studying?”.
Collect the data. This can be done through a sociometric questionnaire, Moreno’s original method, in which each person states who they relate to; through observation; or from digital records (who follows whom, who replies to whom, who wrote with whom).
Represent the network. The data is organised into an adjacency matrix and drawn as a sociogram, the graph that makes the structure visible.
Calculate the metrics. In small networks, the calculations are done by hand; in larger networks, tools such as Gephi or the NetworkX library for the Python language are used.
Interpret. Metrics describe positions, not motives: a value only becomes meaningful when read in the light of the initial question and the context of the group.

To make each step concrete, the rest of this section follows a single example. In a class of nine students, identified from A to I, each student answered the question “Which two classmates would you like to do the next group assignment with?”. There are, therefore, 18 choices in total, two per student.
Sociometric data describes personal relationships and is, by nature, sensitive: knowing that a student was chosen by nobody is information that can hurt or stigmatise. The results should therefore be anonymised, as in this example, and used only for the purpose for which they were collected.

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
section: 3.2 Representing a Social Network as a Graph
text:
3.2 Representing a Social Network as a Graph
Analysing a social network systematically requires, first of all, representing it as a graph: a set of nodes, representing people or organisations, connected by edges, representing their relationships. This is the same representational logic used by Moreno’s sociogram (Section 1.2.1) and by the social and interest graphs discussed in the previous chapter.
An edge, that is, a connection between two nodes, can be undirected, when it represents a mutual, symmetric relationship (for example, a friendship on Facebook, where both parties have to accept the connection), or directed, when it represents a relationship that only holds in one direction (for example, following someone on Instagram or X, which does not imply being followed back). Two people may also have no relationship at all. This distinction matters: most traditional friendship networks (Facebook, LinkedIn) use undirected connections, while most content-centred networks (Instagram, X, YouTube) use directed connections, which has direct implications for the metrics that follow (Figure 3.1).






Figure 3.1: The four types of relationship between two nodes of a social graph.



Edges can also have a weight, which expresses the intensity of the relationship: the number of messages exchanged between two people, the number of times they interacted, or the number of works they wrote together. In a co-authorship network, for example, two authors who signed three chapters together have a connection of weight 3, stronger than that of two authors who collaborated only once. When the weight is not of interest, every edge counts as 1.

3.2.1 From adjacency matrix to sociogram
The simplest way to record the relationships in a network is the adjacency matrix: a table with one row and one column per person, in which the cell in row i and column j is 1 if i chose j, and is left empty otherwise. In the example class, the rows show who chooses and the columns who is chosen (Table 3.1).

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
text:
3.3 Metrics for Social Network Analysis
Network analysis metrics fall into two groups: those that describe the position of each node (who is popular, who is central, who acts as a bridge) and those that describe the network as a whole (how connected, how cohesive, how fragmented). In the definitions that follow, n represents the number of nodes in the network; in the example class, n = 9. Unless otherwise stated, position metrics are calculated on each student’s contacts, regardless of the direction of the choice: A and D are connected whether it was A who chose D or the other way round.

3.3.1 Popularity: in-degree and out-degree
The degree of a node is the number of connections it has. In directed graphs, it is useful to distinguish between connections arriving at a node and connections leaving it. In-degree is the number of connections arriving at a node, and is often used as a direct measure of popularity: on Instagram or X, it corresponds, essentially, to the number of followers. Out-degree is the number of connections leaving a node, corresponding, in that same example, to the number of accounts that user follows, and measures each person’s expansiveness, their tendency to reach out to others.
In the class, in-degree is the last row of the matrix: A and C are the most chosen (4 choices each), followed by F (3); I was chosen by nobody. Out-degree, on the other hand, says nothing in this example: it is 2 for everyone, because the question itself limited each student to two choices. This is a first lesson in method: the way data is collected determines what the metrics are able to reveal.
In the follower network (Figure 3.3), where each account follows whichever accounts it wants, the two degrees already tell different stories. P has five followers and follows only one account, the typical profile of a popular account or a content creator. U follows two accounts and has no followers at all. On real platforms, the difference between the two degrees can span several orders of magnitude: an account may have millions of followers and follow only a few hundred.


3.3.2 Node density
The density of a node measures the proportion between the number of relationships that node actually has and the number it could have, that is, its degree divided by n − 1 (all the other nodes in the network). If a node has only a third of the connections it could have, given the size of the network, its density is approximately 0.33 (Figure 3.6).






Figure 3.6: The same generic five-node network, with different active connections (solid) and possible but non-existent ones (dashed). Density can be calculated for any node; node D is used here as an example: 1, 2 and 4 out of its 4 possible connections, respectively.



In the class, A has contact with four classmates (B, C, D and I) out of a possible eight, a density of 4/8 = 0.50. In the sociogram, six arrows touch A: two going out (A chose B and C) and four coming in (B, C, D and I chose A). The choices with B and with C, however, are reciprocal, and each of those pairs counts as a single contact; A therefore has 4 contacts, not 6. I has contact with two classmates (A and D), a density of 2/8 = 0.25. The density of a node should not be confused with the density of the network, a global metric presented further on (Section 3.3.7).


3.3.3 Centrality as Social Power
Centrality measures how well positioned a node is within the network, which is why it is also called social power. There is no single way to measure centrality: sociologist Linton Freeman proposed, in a work now considered foundational to the field, a conceptual clarification that distinguishes at least three distinct notions of centrality (Freeman 1978):

Degree centrality: how many direct connections a node has. A node with many connections is, on the face of it, more central.
Betweenness centrality: how often a node lies on the shortest path between two other nodes. A node with high betweenness centrality functions as a bridge or broker of information between parts of the network that would otherwise be more distant.
Closeness centrality: how close, on average, a node is to all other nodes in the network. A node with high closeness centrality can reach the rest of the network quickly.

A fourth notion responds to a different intuition: what matters is not only how many contacts one has, but who those contacts are.

Eigenvector centrality: a node is more central the more central the nodes it is connected to (Bonacich 1987). Being connected to two very well-connected people can be worth more than being connected to five isolated people. PageRank, the algorithm Google originally used to rank web pages, rests on the same principle: a page is important if it is linked to by other important pages (Brin and Page 1998).

These four notions capture different aspects of “importance” in a network, and a node can be central by one measure and peripheral by another: a good example is an intermediary who links two distinct communities, but who, within each of them, has few direct connections, low degree centrality, but very high betweenness centrality (Figure 3.7).






Figure 3.7: Each type of centrality highlights a different kind of node: in a star, the node with the most direct connections; in a bridge between two groups, the node connecting the two halves, even with few connections; in a chain, the node positioned closest to all the others.



Centrality values are usually presented on a scale from 0 to 1, which makes it possible to compare nodes with each other. In the class, each measure points to a different student:

in degree, A and C are tied, with four contacts each; dividing by the maximum possible, n − 1 = 8, gives 0.50, the same value as the node density (Section 3.3.2): once normalised, degree centrality is exactly the same calculation as the density of a node;
in betweenness, C leads (0.59), but is closely followed by E (0.54), who has only two contacts: E lies on the only path between the two groups, so any information travelling from one group to the other has to pass through them. The calculation is done by pairs: without E, 8 students remain, and each forms a pair with the other 7, but A-B and B-A are the same pair, giving 8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs. Of these, the ones joining one of the 5 students in {A, B, C, D, I} to one of the 3 in {F, G, H}, 5 × 3 = 15, all pass through E, and 15/28 ≈ 0.54. C reaches 0.59 because it lies on the path between {A, B, D, I} and {E, F, G, H} (16 pairs) and also on half of the B-D pair, which has two shortest paths, one through A and one through C: 16.5/28 ≈ 0.59;
in closeness, C leads again (0.57), being only a few steps away from everyone. Closeness is the inverse of the average distance: add up the distance, in steps, from the node to each of the other n − 1 nodes and compute (n − 1) ÷ sum. C’s distances to the other students are 1 (A, B, D, E), 2 (I, F) and 3 (G, H), adding up to 14, so 8/14 ≈ 0.57. For A the sum is 17 (8/17 ≈ 0.47) and for E it is 15 (8/15 ≈ 0.53): with only two contacts, E is closer to the class than A, because E sits halfway between the two groups;
in eigenvector, A comes first (0.53), because all of A’s contacts (B, C, D, I) are in the denser group, whereas C “spends” one of their connections on E, who has few contacts.



3.3.4 What the metrics mean in a large-scale network
In the class, the metrics are calculated by hand and each value describes a specific student. On a platform such as YouTube or Facebook, with billions of accounts, the same metrics still answer questions about each account’s position, but the scale changes how they are read.
Degree and node density: how many are reached directly. Degree corresponds to the number of subscribers of a YouTube channel or the number of friends of a Facebook profile, and it measures direct reach: the number of people who can see a post without anyone sharing it. The distribution is very unequal: a small number of accounts concentrate millions of connections, while the vast majority have few. Node density, on the other hand, loses its usefulness at platform scale: with billions of accounts, the fraction contacts ÷ (n − 1) is practically zero for everyone, even for a profile with 5,000 friends, the maximum Facebook allows a personal profile. For this reason, node density is calculated within a bounded group, such as a class, a Facebook group or the subscribers of a channel, where it once again shows what share of the group each person knows.
Betweenness: where information flows. On a platform, accounts cluster into communities: the supporters of a club, the players of a game, the followers of a topic. High betweenness belongs to those who connect communities that would otherwise not communicate, such as a content creator who collaborates with channels from other niches, or a user who belongs to two unrelated circles. It is through these accounts that a piece of news, a trend or a piece of misinformation passes from one community to another. If these bridges disappear, each community ends up hearing mostly from its own members, which favours the formation of echo chambers.
Closeness: how quickly everyone is reached. An account with high closeness is only a few steps away from all the others: what it posts can reach the whole network through a few successive shares, and it is also among the first to receive what circulates. These accounts are good starting points for a public health campaign or a product launch. In a large-scale network, however, distances are short for almost everyone, as Milgram’s experiment showed (Section 2.1), so the differences in closeness between accounts are small and only become informative when accounts within the same community are compared.
The social graph is still in use. The sociogram was born in the 1930s, but the structure it draws is still at the heart of many features of today’s platforms. Facebook’s “People You May Know” suggestions take into account, among other factors, mutual friends: this is the logic of the clustering coefficient, according to which two people with contacts in common tend to end up knowing each other. LinkedIn shows the degree of connection next to each profile, 1st, 2nd or 3rd, which is simply the distance in the social graph: a 2nd-degree connection is someone linked to one of your direct connections (LinkedIn 2026). In 2018, Facebook changed its feed to prioritise posts from friends and family over those from public pages (Mosseri 2018). When Twitter, now X, published the code of its recommendation algorithm in 2023, about half of the suggested posts came, on average, from accounts the user follows, ranked by a model that estimates the likelihood of interaction between two people (Twitter Engineering 2023). Measures against misinformation also act on the social graph: WhatsApp began allowing a message to be forwarded to only five chats at a time in 2019, and to a single chat for messages that have already been forwarded many times in 2020, slowing down how fast they spread through the network (WhatsApp 2019, 2020). What has changed is that the social graph no longer stands alone: TikTok relies mainly on the interest graph, and the other platforms combine the two.
There is also a practical issue. Calculating betweenness or closeness requires going through the paths between every pair of accounts, which, with billions of accounts, is impractical. In these networks, the values are estimated from samples of pairs or calculated within smaller communities. In short, degree tells how many people are reached directly, betweenness tells where information flows, and closeness tells how quickly everyone is reached.


3.3.5 Clustering coefficient
The clustering coefficient of a node measures the proportion of pairs of its contacts that are also connected to each other (Watts and Strogatz 1998). It translates the question “are my friends’ friends also my friends?”. A value of 1 indicates that the node belongs to a closed group, in which everyone knows everyone else; a value of 0 indicates that its contacts do not know each other, which is typical of someone who bridges different worlds.
In the class, B has a coefficient of 1: their two contacts, A and C, are connected to each other. E has a coefficient of 0: their contacts, C and F, have no relationship with each other. This is the mechanism platforms exploit when they suggest “people you may know”: if two people have many friends in common, they probably know each other too.


3.3.6 Path and distance
A path between two nodes is any sequence of edges connecting them, directly or indirectly. In a social network, there are typically many possible paths between any two nodes. Distance between two nodes is the length of the shortest path between them, measured by the number of edges traversed. It was precisely this notion of distance that Milgram’s experiment sought to measure empirically (Section 2.1): how many connections, on average, separate two randomly chosen people.
Two global metrics derive from this notion. The diameter is the greatest of the network’s distances, each distance being the shortest path between two nodes: it indicates how long, in the worst case, a piece of information takes to cross it. It is not the longest path one can trace, because by taking detours a longer path can almost always be found. The average distance is the mean of the distances between all pairs of nodes. In the class, the diameter is 5 (from I to H, for example, the shortest path is I, A, C, E, F, H) and the average distance is about 2.4 steps. From I to G the distance is also 5, not 6: the route I, A, C, E, F, H, G exists, but it is not the shortest, because F and G are directly connected.


3.3.7 Network density
Network density measures the proportion between the number of connections that exist in the whole network and the number that would be possible if everyone were connected to everyone. In a directed network with n nodes, each node can choose n − 1 others, so the maximum is n × (n − 1) connections. High-density networks tend to spread information faster, but also to be more susceptible to echo-chamber effects, precisely because almost everyone is connected to almost everyone else.
In the class, there are 18 choices out of a possible 9 × 8 = 72, a density of 18/72 = 0.25. This value, however, requires careful interpretation: since each student could only choose two classmates, 0.25 is the maximum this question allowed. Density is useful for comparing networks collected in the same way (for example, the same class at the start and at the end of the semester), not for comparing networks collected under different rules.
In the follower network, there are 10 connections out of a possible 6 × 5 = 30, a density of 10/30 = 0.33. In an undirected network, each connection serves both nodes at once, so the maximum becomes half: n × (n − 1)/2 connections. In the friendship network, there are 7 friendships out of a possible 6 × 5/2 = 15, a density of 7/15 = 0.47. For the reasons just given, neither of these values should be compared with that of the class.


3.3.8 Reciprocity
In directed networks, reciprocity is the proportion of connections that are returned: if A chooses B, does B also choose A? High reciprocity indicates balanced and stable relationships; low reciprocity is typical of popularity networks, such as follower networks, in which many follow a few without being followed back.
In the class, 12 of the 18 choices are reciprocal (A and B, A and C, B and C, E and F, F and G, G and H), a reciprocity of 0.67. The six unreciprocated choices are equally informative: D chose A and C without being chosen by either, and I chose A and D without being chosen by anyone.
In the follower network (Figure 3.3), only 4 of the 10 connections are reciprocal (P and Q, R and S), a reciprocity of 0.40. P, the most followed account, returns only one of the five follows it receives, the typical pattern of popularity networks.


3.3.9 Components, cliques and subnetworks
A network may be split into several parts with no connection at all between them, called components. Within a component, more cohesive structures can be identified:

a clique is a set of nodes in which everyone is connected to everyone; the smallest is the triangle, with three nodes;
a subnetwork or community is a group of nodes with many connections among themselves and few to the outside; identifying them amounts to finding the “groups” in a network.

The class forms a single component: all the students are connected, even if indirectly. It contains four three-member cliques (A-B-C, A-C-D, A-D-I and F-G-H) and splits into two subnetworks: {A, B, C, D, I} and {E, F, G, H}.


3.3.10 Strong ties, weak ties and structural holes
The previous metrics take on a deeper meaning in the light of two classic theories in the sociology of networks.
Sociologist Mark Granovetter showed that, counter-intuitively, new opportunities (a job, an idea, information not yet circulating in the group) come more often through weak ties, acquaintances and occasional contacts, than through strong ties, close friends and family (Granovetter 1973). The reason is structural: close friends almost all know each other and know more or less the same things; it is weak ties that act as a bridge to other circles, with different information. A bridge is a connection whose removal splits the network into disconnected parts.
Ronald Burt called a structural hole a missing tie between two contacts of the same person: both know that person, but they do not know each other. Whoever sits in between is the broker, and has an advantage: they access information from both sides first and control what passes from one to the other (Burt 1992). A missing tie is not enough for a structural hole: in a network, most possible ties do not exist, and only the one missing between two people with a contact in common counts. Holes are therefore the complement of the clustering coefficient (Section 3.3.5): the coefficient counts the pairs of contacts that are connected, the holes are the pairs that are not. The position of whoever spans holes is the one betweenness centrality measures.
In the class, E has a clustering coefficient of 0: their two contacts, C and F, are not connected, and E spans that hole. C also spans holes, because C is the only member of their group connected to E, and C even has the highest betweenness in the class. Both lie on the only path between the groups: the C-E and E-F connections are the only two bridges in the network, and if C or E is absent, or changes class, the two groups no longer have any connection at all. The difference lies in the rest of the position: C is well embedded in their own group, whereas E has nothing but the hole, with just two contacts who do not know each other. E is the broker between the two subnetworks in the purest sense: their importance comes entirely from the position between the groups.
The message network (Figure 3.4) shows the same idea with weights. With only three messages in a week, the connection between Carla and Duarte is by far the weakest tie in the network, but it is also the only bridge between the two groups: if it disappeared, no information would pass from one group to the other.
Finally, subnetworks rarely form by chance. Homophily is people’s tendency to connect with others similar to themselves, in age, interests, opinions or background (McPherson, Smith-Lovin, and Cook 2001). It helps explain why closed groups form and, on digital platforms, why recommendation algorithms, by suggesting content and contacts similar to those one already has, tend to reinforce echo chambers.

Read together, the metrics tell a story that none of them tells on its own:

A is the most popular student in the larger group and the best connected to classmates who are themselves well connected (highest eigenvector centrality), but hardly acts as a bridge for anyone.
C is equally popular and, in addition, holds the most strategic position in the class: closest to everyone and appearing most often on the paths between classmates.
E is the most interesting case: chosen only once and with just two contacts, but the broker between the two subnetworks. An analysis based on popularity alone would never have singled them out.
I has an in-degree of zero: they chose two classmates and were chosen by neither. They are not isolated, since they have outgoing connections, but their position deserves attention.

Interpretation nonetheless requires caution. Metrics describe positions in a network, not intentions or personal qualities. The question put to the class only collected positive choices: the fact that nobody chose I does not mean I is rejected, only that they are not among anyone’s first preferences. Moreno, precisely for this reason, also asked “who would you not like to work with?” (Moreno 1934). A good analysis always returns to the start of the method: what question was asked, to whom, and what the data does, or does not, allow one to conclude.

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
text:
3.5 Folksonomy: Collective Content Classification
So far, this chapter has dealt with how to analyse relationships between people. But much of the structure of a modern social network also results from how content is classified and organised, and this is where folksonomy comes in.
The term folksonomy was coined by Thomas Vander Wal in 2007, from the combination of folk (people) and taxonomy (Vander Wal 2007). It denotes the classification of content through a free, collective tagging process, rather than a hierarchy of categories defined a priori by domain experts.
The difference from a traditional taxonomy is structural: in a taxonomy, a group of managers defines a hierarchy of categories in advance, and all content has to fit into it. In a folksonomy, there is no such prior hierarchy: categories, or tags, emerge as users themselves classify content, with no centralised control.
The tagging process can be represented simply: a group of people, or a single person, associates a set of tags with a set of objects (documents, images, posts) (Figure 3.8). Because different people classify the same object in different ways, according to their own perspective, the resulting folksonomy is rich and heterogeneous, but can also contain inconsistencies.






Figure 3.8: The tagging process: people associate free tags with objects, with no hierarchy defined in advance.



Two types of folksonomy can be distinguished (Vander Wal 2007): broad folksonomy, in which a large number of users tag the same objects, which is useful for identifying the most popular items in a collection, and narrow folksonomy, in which only one or a few people tag each object, typically the content’s own author, which preserves a more personal vocabulary, but makes discovery by others harder.
A common way to visualise the aggregate result of a folksonomy is the tag cloud, a representation in which the most-used tags stand out, typically in larger or darker type, making it possible to quickly identify the dominant themes of a collection (Figure 3.9).






Figure 3.9: Tag cloud: the larger and darker the tag, the more often it was used in the collection.




3.5.1 Advantages and problems
Folksonomy has clear advantages: it does not depend on domain experts to define categories, it lets each user classify freely without having to learn a controlled vocabulary, and it captures the real vocabulary of those who actually use the system, not that of those who designed it.
But that same freedom generates well-documented problems: spelling mistakes, morphological variation (for example, “social network” and “social networks” recorded as distinct tags), synonymy (different terms for the same concept), polysemy (the same term with different meanings depending on context), and clutter from low-relevance tags. Current platforms partially mitigate these problems with automatic spell-checking, suggestions of tags already used by others, and semi-automatic grouping of semantically close tags.

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
section: 3.6 Folksonomy in Practice: from Tags to Hashtags
text:
3.6 Folksonomy in Practice: from Tags to Hashtags
When the concept of folksonomy became popular, around 2007, the reference examples were systems such as Amazon, YouTube, Flickr and Del.icio.us. It is worth understanding, concretely, how the same idea, free content tagging, produced very different results depending on who was allowed to tag.
On Amazon, until the feature was discontinued in 2013, any customer could attach free tags to a product: the same book could be tagged by different customers as “science fiction”, “dystopia” or “beach read”. Because tagging was open to the entire customer base, a broad folksonomy formed: many voices classifying the same object, which made the most repeated tags a reasonable indicator of collective consensus about what that product actually is.
On YouTube, the mechanism is the opposite, and remains so today: only whoever publishes a video can attach tags to it, through YouTube Studio. Whoever merely watches the video takes no part in its classification. It is, therefore, a narrow folksonomy: it reflects the personal perspective of whoever published the content, not a collective consensus among those who consume it.
Del.icio.us too, a social bookmarking service that let people organise and share web sites through tags, no longer exists: after changing owners several times, it stopped accepting new bookmarks in 2017, when it was acquired by competitor Pinboard, which turned it into a read-only archive.
The mechanism, however, survived the change of platforms, just under another name: the hashtag. By attaching a tag preceded by “#” to a post on Instagram, TikTok or X, each user is taking part in exactly the same collective tagging process described by Vander Wal almost two decades before these platforms came to dominate the market. A study on Instagram hashtags shows precisely that: the folksonomy generated by users through hashtags can be modelled as a complex network, linking posts and profiles that share the same themes, with no central coordination whatsoever among those who use them (Ibba et al. 2015).
The hashtag also inherits the same tensions as classic folksonomy: on Instagram, a popular hashtag like #food has a broad folksonomy, with millions of contributors, but little value for finding something specific; a niche hashtag, created by a small community for a specific event or narrow interest, works more like a narrow folksonomy, more precise, but also less discoverable by those who do not already know about it.

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
text:
3.7 Summary
This chapter developed two complementary tools for understanding the structure of social networks:

Social Network Analysis studies the structure of relationships between people and follows five steps: define the question and the boundary of the network, collect the data, represent it as an adjacency matrix and a sociogram, calculate metrics and interpret them (Wasserman and Faust 1994)
A social network can be represented as a graph, with directed or undirected edges, weighted or unweighted, depending on the type of relationship
The position metrics of a node are in-degree (popularity) and out-degree, node density, degree, betweenness, closeness (Freeman 1978) and eigenvector centrality (Bonacich 1987), and the clustering coefficient
The global metrics of the network are average distance and diameter, network density, reciprocity, and the division into components, cliques and subnetworks
Weak ties and the brokers who span structural holes link groups that would otherwise not communicate (Granovetter 1973; Burt 1992)
Metrics describe positions, not intentions: their interpretation always depends on the question that produced the data
Folksonomy is the collective classification of content through free tagging, distinct from a hierarchical taxonomy defined a priori (Vander Wal 2007)
Broad and narrow folksonomy represent a trade-off between reach and precision of classification
The hashtag is the contemporary form of folksonomy, present in practically every current social network (Ibba et al. 2015)

title: 3  Social Networks: Metrics and Folksonomy
text:
3.8 Food for Thought
Think of a social network you use often: among the people you follow, can you identify someone with high betweenness centrality, that is, someone who links groups of people who would not otherwise be in contact? If you drew the sociogram of your class from the question “who do you ask for help when studying?”, which students would you expect to find with high in-degree, and which with high betweenness? Would they be the same?
And what about the hashtags you use or follow: are they broad folksonomy, a generic tag used by millions of people, or narrow folksonomy, specific to a small community? What problems of synonymy or morphological variation have you already noticed in hashtags (for example, two different spellings of the same topic splitting the same conversation into two)?
